issues.legal_issue: A co-sharer’s non-participation in the rents and profits of jointly held land does not by itself amount to ouster or give another co-sharer title by adverse possession.
material_facts: The parties were recorded as co-bhumidars and had held a joint khewat.
The defendants managed the land while the plaintiff lived elsewhere; she said they gave her shares from time to time and assured her that her interest would be protected.
The defendants claimed separate occupation, but the District Judge found no evidence that the plaintiff had not received a share of the produce and no clear ouster was established.
issues.conclusion: The defendants’ possession was in law also the plaintiff’s possession. Mere non-participation in rents and profits did not oust her or give the defendants title by adverse possession; the defendants’ position was also in the nature of constructive trustees for her.
issues.legal_principle: A co-sharer’s mere non-participation in rents and profits does not constitute ouster sufficient to establish the other co-sharer’s title by adverse possession. In that situation, the co-sharer in possession is treated as a constructive trustee for the other co-sharer, whose possession is protected through that relationship. No particular statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this principle.

rule.if: co_sharer_possession_dispute and joint_co_ownership and not clear_ouster

predicates.co_sharer_possession_dispute: The dispute concerns a co-owner’s claimed right to possession of jointly held land against another co-owner.
predicates.joint_co_ownership: The parties held the land jointly as co-owners.
predicates.clear_ouster: The co-owner in possession clearly excluded the other co-owner from possession.

issues.definition: When co-owners dispute possession and joint ownership exists without clear exclusion, non-participation in the land’s returns does not establish adverse title against the absent co-owner.

issues.legal_issue: A civil suit to establish title is not barred after consolidation unless the statute expressly bars that suit or the claim is one that could be made under the statute’s procedures.
material_facts: After consolidation, the plaintiff sued for joint possession of her claimed share in two plots.
The High Court held that the suit was barred after completion of consolidation proceedings.
The plaintiff sought to establish her title, and the Court found no applicable express bar to that title-based suit.
issues.conclusion: The suit was not barred, and the High Court erred in holding otherwise.
issues.legal_principle: Courts do not readily infer a bar to a suit to establish title without an express statutory provision. The Court relied on Subha Singh v. Mahendra Singh, A.I.R. 1974 S.C. 1657, which held that a claim not capable of being brought under the relevant statute’s procedures did not attract the statutory bar to civil-court jurisdiction over title.

rule.if: title_based_civil_suit and post_consolidation_dispute and not express_suit_bar

predicates.title_based_civil_suit: A party brings a civil suit seeking to establish title to land.
predicates.post_consolidation_dispute: The suit is brought after land-consolidation proceedings have concluded.
predicates.express_suit_bar: The statute expressly bars the civil suit seeking to establish title.

issues.definition: A title-based civil suit brought after consolidation is not barred when no express bar applies.

issues.legal_issue: A court hearing a second appeal cannot overturn factual findings made by the first appellate court on the evidence merely by re-evaluating those facts.
material_facts: The District Judge, after considering the evidence, found that the plaintiff’s name had been removed from the records through fraud, that she had not been shown to have received no share of the produce, and that she was not informed of consolidation proceedings and had relied on the defendants’ assurances.
The High Court reversed the District Judge’s decree in a second appeal, including by treating the evidence and the alleged fraud differently.
The Supreme Court held that the District Judge’s findings were findings of fact and that the High Court had also made an error of record about the plaintiff’s evidence.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not entitled to interfere with the District Judge’s factual findings in second appeal, and its contrary findings could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the District Judge’s findings on the evidence were findings of fact binding in second appeal and not open to interference by the High Court. The judgment cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this rule.

predicates.second_appeal_proceeding: The matter before the reviewing court is a second appeal.
predicates.first_appellate_court_made_evidence_base: The first appellate court made factual findings after considering the evidence.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, evidence-based factual findings made by the first appellate court cannot be reweighed by the reviewing court.

issues.legal_issue: A claim that one co-owner misled another into entrusting property management is distinct from a claim that fraud was practised on consolidation authorities.
material_facts: The plaintiff said she left management of the jointly held property to the defendants after they assured her that her share would be protected, and that they did not inform her of the consolidation proceedings.
The District Judge accepted her account and found that her name had been deliberately dropped from the revenue records.
The High Court proceeded on the basis that no fraud had been shown against the consolidation authorities, while the plaintiff’s case was that the defendants had practised fraud on her.
issues.conclusion: The High Court misunderstood the plaintiff’s case: it concerned fraud against her, not fraud on the consolidation authorities, and its reasoning on that basis was unsound.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished an allegation that a party was deceived by others who undertook to protect her interests from an allegation that the authorities themselves were defrauded. The judgment cited no specific statutory provision or earlier case for this distinction.

predicates.co_ownership_management_dispute: The dispute concerns management of property jointly owned by the claimant and the other party.
predicates.reliance_on_management_assurances: The claimant entrusted management to the other party after receiving assurances that the claimant’s interest would be protected.
predicates.fraud_claim_targets_the_claimant: The claimant alleges that the other party deceived the claimant, rather than alleging fraud on the decision-making authorities.

issues.definition: When a claimant entrusted jointly owned property to another based on assurances and alleges deception against the claimant, the absence of an allegation of fraud on authorities does not defeat that claim.
